title: Someone Who Got There First
description:
An investment seminar. The presenter stepped up.

"Hi, I'm Lee Minseo. I started in a Gangnam jeonse apartment [rented deposit-only] at 35, and now I own the place outright. I'm 38."

[Jeonse: Korea's unique deposit-only rental system. Instead of monthly rent, you pay a large lump-sum (often 100 million won-500M+) that sits with the landlord. No monthly payments. At lease end, you get the full deposit back. It's how many Koreans 'step into' expensive areas without buying.]

Started at 35. Goal reached at 38. Three years.

{name} ran the numbers. That timeline is almost identical to his.

choices.text: Get her business card after the talk — want to ask how
choices.result_text:
Lee Minseo smiled and handed over her card.

A handshake with someone who owns a Gangnam apartment. Slightly unreal. And — she was once standing where {name} is standing.

choices.text: Just listened and left — no nerve to approach
choices.result_text:
On the way home, her words kept running through his head.

Not 'it can be done' — but 'she already did it.' That stayed longer than expected.

title: Beyond Gangnam
description:
Ran into Lee Minseo at a café near the seminar venue. Different face than on stage.

"Oh — you were at the seminar, weren't you?"

Coffee together. She said things she didn't say at the talk.

"Honestly — I got more exhausted after buying the apartment. There's the mortgage. Kids' tutoring costs. And even though the price went up, I can't sell — I live there."

Got Gangnam — and Gangnam got her.

choices.text: "But you achieved the goal." — see the positive
choices.result_text:
Lee Minseo smiled briefly. "Yes. I did achieve it."

But that smile was different somehow. {name} wanted to understand the difference. Probably have to get there to know.

choices.text: "Is there something I'm not seeing? Tell me honestly." — ask directly
choices.result_text:
She thought for a moment, then said:
"When you have a goal — you have to be ready for when the goal disappears. That's the hardest part."

It took {name} a while to understand what that meant.

title: The One Who Arrives
description:
Gangnam wasn't far now.

With the number nearly full, a message came from Lee Minseo.
"I heard. They say you're almost there."

They met again at that same cafe.
"Congratulations. I mean it."
Then she went quiet for a moment.
"Remember what I told you back then?"

{name} remembered. 'When you have a goal, prepare for when it disappears.'
Now — he was starting to understand what she meant.

choices.text: "I think I'm starting to get it." — said it honestly
choices.result_text:
Lee Minseo nodded.
"Right? When you arrive, the next question comes. 'So now what.'
But that's not all bad. At least — it's a new question."

For the first time, {name} felt that Gangnam wasn't the end, but the start of the next sentence.

choices.text: "I haven't arrived yet. Don't want to count my chickens." — smiled
choices.result_text:
Lee Minseo laughed. "Fair enough. See it all the way through."

Still, {name} decided to tuck her words away in his bag.
He'd take them out once he got there.

It was Minjun who had reached out first, using that business card.
Not because he had a question — because he needed someone to ask.

title: Even If You Don't Arrive
description:
Gangnam was still far off. The number hadn't filled.

And then Minseo reached out.
"How are you holding up? Almost there?"

Minjun answered honestly. Still far. Maybe he wouldn't make it at all.

Minseo was quiet a moment, then said,
"Remember what I told you? To prepare for when the goal disappears."
"...Yeah."
"Here's the thing — even if you don't reach the goal, you need that same preparation. The one who arrives and the one who doesn't. In the end the question left over is the same."
"What question?"
"Whether that goal was ever really yours."

choices.result_text:
Minseo smiled.
"Then you're fine. Arriving is a separate problem."

He hung up and looked out the window. Gangnam was still far away.
But strangely — today the distance didn't ache the way it used to.

Minseo didn't scold the answer.
"Asking that even now — that puts you ahead of the ones who arrived."

Minjun held the phone for a long time.
Even if he never reached Gangnam, what he shouldn't lose along the way — he was starting to understand it, a little.

title: The Cost Sheet After Arrival
description:
At 11:30 Saturday morning, Minseo entered the cafe near the seminar at the time {name} had arranged. In {name}'s bag, the R4-SELF contract and the clinic copy from the previous day shared one clear folder. Minseo offered neither congratulations nor consolation. She turned her calculator facedown and asked,

“The contract has a loss cap. How much of your day can you lose before you stop?”

{name} began to explain whether he had reached the goal, then closed his mouth. Minseo drew three boxes on a napkin—money, body, people—and pushed it over while they were still blank. “Not your balance. Write one price you've already paid.” As the foam sank in his coffee, {name} chose one box he could no longer keep hidden.

choices.text: Place the fourteen-day sleep record he had with him in the body box
choices.result_text:
{name} unfolded the fourteen-day sleep record he had with him and turned its daily sleep columns toward Minseo. She did not enter the figures into her calculator.

“That's principal, not yield. If the principal is wearing away while you count only returns, the ledger is lying.”

{name} folded the sleep record again. The crease ran through the body box, leaving only dates and sleep times on the sheet.

choices.text: Place the R4-SELF he had opened with Daeun in the people box, turned to the weekend-and-night clause
choices.result_text:
{name} took out the R4-SELF he had opened with Daeun and set it down with the weekend-and-night clause visible. Minseo read the sentence containing those two words slowly.

“That's not time spent on a person. It's a contract spending the time that belonged to one. Those use different arithmetic.”

Minseo did not say Daeun's name aloud. The cafe light narrowed over the words weekend and night.

choices.text: Write the 70 million won gap in the money box
choices.result_text:
{name} wrote 70 million won in the money box and added the Friday deadline. Minseo asked, “When you fill that figure, what goes in the next blank?”

{name} had no immediate answer. Minseo left the napkin open beneath her cup. Only the money box was dark with ink; the body and people boxes remained empty at the edge of the coffee ring.

title: The Sheet Before a Diagnosis
description:
At 9:20 Friday morning, {name} sat in the family-medicine exam room he had booked. On the desk lay fourteen days of sleep records, a blank form for the times his hand trembled, and a blood-pressure slip. The doctor looked at {name}'s hands before the monitor and capped the pen.

“I won't name this from one screen. Choose the information we must not leave out: sleep, tremors, or the hours you worked.”

A registration band was already fastened around {name}'s wrist. He had to slide one set of records across without hiding it. A queue number sounded once in the corridor, and fluorescent light spread over the still-empty diagnosis field.

choices.text: Hand over all fourteen days of sleep records with the dates visible
choices.result_text:
{name} handed over all fourteen days instead of selecting only the nights he slept well. The doctor circled the nights below four hours and left a field beside them for follow-up.

No diagnosis was added. The stamped copy held only dense rows of sleep and waking times. {name} folded it in half and placed it in the clear folder.

choices.text: Show the hand-tremor videos with their timestamps
choices.result_text:
{name} played three videos of his hand trembling around a water bottle, keeping each timestamp visible. The doctor paused the images to ask about caffeine and meal intervals, leaving unanswered fields blank.

Instead of a confirmed name, three observation times entered the form. When the phone went dark, a steady hand appeared briefly in the black glass.

choices.text: Open the contract calendar and the hours actually worked
choices.result_text:
{name} hid the income figures and contract names, then showed the start and finish times from the last four weeks. The doctor marked the blocks past midnight and the missing meals in different colors.

“You don't have to discuss the money. We do need the hours your body worked.”

The clinic copy held time without amounts. Neither color skipped a single week.

title: Not Whatever Day Is Left
description:
At 7:40 Sunday evening, {name} unfolded the napkin on which Minseo had drawn three boxes. Only the box he had chosen before Minseo held one trace—a figure, the folded sleep record, or the open weekend-and-night clause; the other two remained blank. Pressing the space between the three boxes with one finger, {name} asked,

“After three billion won, what kind of day should we still protect together?”

Daeun did not answer at once. She turned her phone facedown and pulled the weekend-and-night clause from R4-SELF beside the napkin.

“Minjun, don't give me time left after you've counted all the money. Tell me what time is mine from the beginning. Then I'll tell you what I would give up for it.”

The question had already been asked. {name} had to take one real boundary from the calendar.

choices.text: Say one evening a week will take no contract calls
choices.result_text:
{name} pointed to one Thursday evening. Daeun did not begin by believing the word every.

“Leave this Thursday open first. If you don't keep it, don't stop at saying you were busy. Tell me what you chose instead.”

{name} drew a slash through the contract-alert block after seven. No number showed the money lost, but two hours that could not be sold appeared on the calendar for the first time.

choices.text: Say one Sunday a month will be blocked first, not left over
choices.result_text:
{name} circled the first Sunday of the next month. Daeun opened her schedule to the same date but did not mark the promise complete.

“I don't want a day you meet me because it happened to remain. If you leave it open first, I'll check what I would have to clear that day too.”

The same date glowed on both screens. Daeun set her phone facedown beside the napkin instead of marking anything complete.

choices.text: Say a call about health or family will stop the calculation first
choices.result_text:
{name} drew one line between the clinic form and the family-call entry. Daeun did not nod; she wrote ‘tell me before’ in the people box.

“Explaining after you collapse isn't protecting something together. Let me know before you stop too.”

Neither of them folded the paper until the blue ink dried. The calculator screen went dark first.
